specPoints.text: describe the stages of protein synthesis including transcription and translation, including the role of mRNA, ribosomes, tRNA, codons and anticodons

primer.text: One gene, one protein, two stages between them. This note walks transcription inside the nucleus — unwind, expose, bind, join, exit — and translation on the ribosome — dock, match, bond, stop — naming the roles of mRNA, tRNA, codons and anticodons that the mark scheme rewards.

lessons.title: Transcription in the Nucleus
lessons.opening: Protein synthesis runs in two stages: transcription in the nucleus copies a gene into single-stranded mRNA, and translation in the cytoplasm reads that message into a chain of amino acids on the ribosome.
keyPoints: Transcription happens in the nucleus and produces a strand of mRNA.
Hydrogen bonds break so the DNA unwinds and exposes the template strand.
Free mRNA nucleotides bind their complementary partners on the template.
The finished mRNA leaves the nucleus through a pore.

low.restatement: The nucleus photocopies the gene's instructions onto an mRNA strand.
low.analogy: Copying one recipe page in the library and sending the copy to the kitchen.
low.examPointer: Keep the order of the five steps firm; sequence questions are common.

medium.restatement: Complementary binding is what preserves the message: each template base dictates its partner.
medium.analogy: A lock-and-key pass along the template, one base at a time.
medium.examPointer: Say complementary copy, not identical copy; the pairing rule matters.

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

Ribosomes receive the mRNA after transcription.
Mitochondria are not part of this account.

tRNA is a separate working type.

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

check.stem: How does the mRNA strand relate to the template?

options.text: Its bases mirror the template strand, base for complementary base
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: An identical clone of the template
options.explanation: Pairing makes it complementary, not identical.
The copy preserves the sequence faithfully.
Nothing reverses during transcription.

check.stem: How does the mRNA reach the cytoplasm?

options.text: Through a pore in the nuclear envelope
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The molecule travels intact.
No such mechanism is taught.
tRNA works later, in translation.

check.stem: List the five transcription steps in order.
check.modelAnswer: The DNA unwinds, the template strand is exposed, free mRNA nucleotides bind, the nucleotides join into a single strand, and the mRNA leaves through a pore.
Transcription is the nuclear stage that copies a section of DNA into a strand of mRNA.

check.stem: Explain why the mRNA must leave the nucleus for the next stage.
check.modelAnswer: Ribosomes sit in the cytoplasm, so the message has to travel out of the nucleus before translation can begin.

check.stem: A poison blocks the pores in the nuclear envelope of a cell. Describe the effect on protein synthesis.
check.modelAnswer: mRNA can no longer leave the nucleus, so it never reaches the ribosomes in the cytoplasm and translation cannot start.

lessons.title: Translation on the Ribosome
lessons.opening: Translation converts the message into protein: the mRNA docks on a ribosome, tRNA molecules match their anticodons to the codons, amino acids link by peptide bonds, and a stop codon releases the finished chain for folding.
keyPoints: Translation occurs in the cytoplasm on ribosomes.
Each tRNA carries an anticodon at one end and an amino acid at the other.
Anticodons pair with complementary codons on the mRNA.
Peptide bonds join neighbouring amino acids as the chain grows.
A stop codon ends translation and the chain folds into its protein.

low.restatement: The message is read three bases at a time, and each matching tRNA drops off its amino acid.
low.analogy: A bead stringer reads the instruction card and collects matching beads one by one.
low.examPointer: Pair the terms: codon on mRNA, anticodon on tRNA.

medium.restatement: The fixed anticodon-codon correspondence is what keeps the protein faithful to the gene.
medium.analogy: A bilingual dictionary where each word maps to exactly one translation.
medium.examPointer: Name the stop codon as the signal that releases the finished chain.

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The nucleus hosts transcription only.
The pore is a doorway, not a workshop.
The membrane is not a translation site.

check.stem: What does each tRNA molecule carry?

options.text: An anticodon triplet and its specific amino acid
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
tRNA carries one amino acid, not a gene.
tRNA is a single-stranded molecule.
The amino acid is the cargo.

check.stem: What pairs with a codon on the mRNA?

options.text: The complementary anticodon of a tRNA
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Codons pair with anticodons, not each other.
DNA stays in the nucleus.
Bonds join amino acids; they do not pair with codons.

check.stem: What joins the amino acids together?

options.text: Peptide bonds between neighbouring amino acids
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Those held the DNA strands, not the protein chain.
Phosphates belong to the nucleic acid backbone.
Fibres pull chromosomes, not amino acids.

check.stem: What signals the end of translation?

options.text: A stop codon on the mRNA
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Depletion is not the taught signal.
Ribosomes are not the signal source.

options.text: The nucleus calling the chain back
options.explanation: The nucleus is not involved here.

check.modelAnswer: Translation is the cytoplasm stage where the mRNA is read on ribosomes and an amino acid chain is produced.

check.stem: State the roles of codon and anticodon.
check.modelAnswer: The codon is the mRNA triplet and the anticodon is the matching tRNA triplet that brings the specified amino acid.

check.stem: Explain why each anticodon corresponds to exactly one amino acid.
check.modelAnswer: The matching rule between anticodon and codon is fixed, so each tRNA delivers the same amino acid every time, keeping the protein sequence faithful to the gene.

check.stem: A mutation changes a codon on an mRNA into a stop codon. Predict the effect on the protein produced.
check.modelAnswer: Translation halts at that codon, so the amino acid chain is cut short and the finished protein is incomplete.

glossary.definition: The nuclear stage copying a gene into a strand of mRNA.
The cytoplasm stage reading mRNA on ribosomes into an amino acid chain.
A triplet of bases on mRNA that specifies one amino acid.
The matching triplet on tRNA that pairs with a codon.
The link joining neighbouring amino acids during translation.
